newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ foreign minister sees Iran row solved this week.
newsitem.headline: NZ foreign minister sees Iran row solved this week.

text.p: New Zealand's foreign minister said on Tuesday he expected a rapid resolution of a confused diplomatic row with Iran that has included the threat of a trade ban on New Zealand by Tehran.
Don McKinnon told Radio New Zealand he was still not sure Iran had cut off trade relations, a move sparked by a German court ruling linking Iran to terrorism.
"I think by the end of the week it will be resolved. So far, as I understand it, it's not affecting any New Zealand exports", he said.
McKinnon's comment added to the uncertainty of the last 24 hours when the two countries' diplomats in Wellington have issued conflicting statements about trade relations.
On Monday evening the Iranian embassy had appeared to confirm that the trade ban, first reported by the official news agency IRNA on Saturday, was already in place.
It had also announced ambassador Mohammad Sazegara would be recalled on Tuesday for consultations in a mirror of the action taken by New Zealand on Friday.
The statement said that Iran, through Construction Jihad Minister Gholamreza Forouzesh, "has ordered the suspension of all trade agreements with New Zealand parties until further notice".

Later on Monday evening, however, McKinnon issued a statement after meeting Sazegara that said: "The ambassador has told me he has not received any formal advice from Iran that a trade ban has been put in place against New Zealand. I am very pleased to receive that information."
On Tuesday it was still not possible to clarify the exact status of the trade ban, and the Iranian embassy said Sazegara had returned to Tehran as planned.
The two groups of diplomats have used some conciliatory language throughout, and implied they wish to restore relations through dialogue.
McKinnon reconfirmed New Zealand's intention to send its ambassador to Iran, Daniel Richards, back to Tehran by the end of this week.
Richards was recalled when New Zealand joined in a concerted international response to a German court ruling that Iran had ordered the 1992 murders of four Kurdish dissidents in Berlin.

The Iranian embassy statement also referred to the prospect of dialogue to smooth over relations later this week. Sazegara would seek to meet his New Zealand counterpart Richards in a few days' time, it said.
The two hoped "to meet and discuss with Iranian authorities...with a view to normalising the relations between both countries on the basis of mutual respect", it added.
Since the row broke out at the weekend, some of New Zealand's primary exporters have expressed concerns about the effects of a full-scale ban on their agricultural produce trade.

The trade, mainly selling lamb, dairy produce and wool to Iran, is not large in overall terms, totalling an estimated NZ$170 million ($119 million) last year. But if suspended it could cause short-term problems, producers said.
